extracted.intended_audience: research mathematicians (number theorists and arithmetic geometers), readers of Mochizuki's IUT papers, journal editors and referees
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and practical advice for judging the correctness, clarity, and publishability of a long, technical mathematical proof (here applied to Mochizuki's IUT papers). Focuses on exposition, dependencies, verifiability of key steps, and editorial/refereeing responsibilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity and economy of new terminology
rubrics_metrics.description: The first couple hundred pages introduce a lot of difficult new terminology; Scholze and Stix demonstrated that none of this new terminology is necessary to prove any of the formal statements in these pages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid dressing up simple statements in confusing and difficult terminology. New terminology should provide genuine conceptual or technical leverage; if statements compress to simpler known arguments when the new language is removed, that is evidence the terminology is unnecessary and harms clarity. Editors/referees should be skeptical when a manuscript uses very large amounts of novel notation/terminology without clear necessity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verifiability of key points by independent readers
rubrics_metrics.description: Many people read the papers and understood early parts but were unable to verify a key point – Corollary 3.12; large numbers of readers getting stuck at the same point is worrying.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Central claims must be presented so independent experts can check them; it is not normal for many competent readers to stall on the same step. If many readers fail at the same place, either the paper needs clearer explanation or the argument is flawed. Authors should restructure or expand proofs where many readers get stuck.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial and refereeing duty to ensure clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: As an editor or referee, you should ensure papers are clear and get to the point; allowing a paper to be published whose arguments cause most serious readers to get stuck is a failure of editorial duty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journals should demand adequate explanation of critical steps and not rely on an inner circle to rescue explanations post-publication. Editors should not only accept referees who are favorable; they should ensure rigorous, independent verification and clarity. If a paper's exposition can be substantially compressed by removing unnecessary terminology, editors should question the presentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear justification of central corollaries/statements
rubrics_metrics.description: Corollary 3.12 is singled out as a point that many cannot verify; missing or unclear justification of such central statements undermines the overall claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should either give a detailed, checkable proof of central corollaries or replace them with a sequence of simpler lemmas each with explicit proofs. Don't leave a key inequality or corollary only as an asserted consequence without transparent derivation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparent handling of dependencies on prior work
rubrics_metrics.description: The papers reference many prior papers (EtTh, AAGX, AAG1-3, etc.); dependence chains are long and opaque, making it hard to see which inputs are essential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should clearly document which prior results are used and whether those inputs are independent or can be avoided. If the argument relies on many earlier papers, explain modularly which parts of those papers are invoked and provide brief self-contained statements or reductions so the reader need not reconstruct a long dependency chain to check the argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respond to objections with precise clarifications
rubrics_metrics.description: When precise objections are raised (e.g., Scholze and Stix's objection), the author's response should make concrete clarifications or edits rather than arguing in generalities that 'an argument like this could work'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If readers point out a plausible flaw or ambiguity, provide explicit corrections, clarifications, or rewrites that resolve the issue. Avoid only asserting that critics misunderstood; instead produce concrete, checkable amendments or decompositions of the proof that address the objection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid over-invoking global baggage; prefer modular/simpler assertions
rubrics_metrics.description: Some propositions invoke 'too much structure' and could be broken into many simpler assertions each of which can be individually checked.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decompose complex statements into minimal hypotheses and modular lemmas. Reduce reliance on the 'full base hodge theater' or similar heavy baggage when local/functorial interpretations suffice. Present smaller, verifiable steps rather than a single opaque giant claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explicitness of diagrams, maps, and commutativity claims
rubrics_metrics.description: The threads emphasize the need to show where diagrams commute and where indeterminacies are used; many arguments refer to diagrams without explicit maps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give explicit diagrams with maps labeled, state precisely what commutes and whether commutativity holds up to specified indeterminacies; if 'commutes up to indeterminacy' is invoked, define the indeterminacy and demonstrate how it affects the argument. Do not rely on vague schematic pictures alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justify and explain indeterminacies (ind1, ind2, ind3)
rubrics_metrics.description: The role of ind1, ind2, ind3 (the indeterminacies) must be made clear: e.g., ind2 'mixes valuations' only so much and ind3 is needed to make formulas work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State exactly why each indeterminacy is introduced and where each is essential in the deductions. If some indeterminacy preserves certain submodules or annuli (so it 'does not do too much'), explain the consequences for the constructions and why stronger indeterminacies are necessary elsewhere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain how theta-values are recovered from Galois/fundamental groups
rubrics_metrics.description: Several commenters ask how Galois groups or pi1's can 'interpret' theta-values; the mechanism is not made clear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide a concrete account (or pointer to one) of the reconstruction procedure that recovers q and Theta functions from the fundamental group, including the role of etale theta-functions and any anabelian theorems invoked. If such recovery is crucial for the proof, include explicit steps or references sufficient for verification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarify the nature and role of log-links and gluing
rubrics_metrics.description: Discussion centers on whether log-links are about monoids or pi1's, how gluing Hodge theaters along log-links affects ring structures, and when identity gluing is inconsistent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define log-links precisely, state which data they identify and which they leave indeterminate, and show (with examples if helpful) how gluing affects local/global structures (e.g., 'holomorphic' or ring structures). Address whether gluing by identity is allowable and where full poly-isomorphisms are required to obtain consistency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make concrete inequalities and numerical factors explicit
rubrics_metrics.description: Scholze and Stix's objection alleges a numerical discrepancy (off by factor j^2) in a claimed inequality; such concrete factors must be settled explicitly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a proof hinges on a quantitative inequality, give an explicit chain of implications and bounds where each numerical factor is tracked. If a claimed improvement over a trivial inequality is by a specific factor, show precisely where that gain arises and justify it rigorously.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be explicit about which monoids/structures are identified across constructions
rubrics_metrics.description: There are many monoids built into the theory; it's unclear which are implicitly assumed to be identified in statements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: List the monoids and other algebraic structures used in each construction, and state whether and why they are to be identified across different theaters/links. If some identifications are optional, explain the consequences of choosing or not choosing them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publish transparent edited versions or editorial notes
rubrics_metrics.description: The commenter suggests the author or journal could post that Corollary 3.12 has been replaced or rewritten with detailed proofs to reduce criticism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain transparent public versions showing substantial edits or clarifications; if a central claim is revised, state how it was replaced (e.g., 'Corollary 3.12 replaced by X lemmas totaling Y pages with detailed proofs'). This helps the community assess whether objections have been addressed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid vague, psychological language; define terms precisely
rubrics_metrics.description: Phrases like 'history of groups' or psychological remarks about what Mochizuki 'surprised' him are unhelpful; precise technical definitions are needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Replace metaphorical or psychological language with formal definitions and precise statements. When rhetorical or philosophical comments are made, separate them clearly from rigorous mathematical claims to avoid confusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical refereeing: avoid selective citation of favorable referees
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors should not avoid criticism by finding only referees who will endorse a paper; such practices raise ethical concerns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refereeing should be independent and fair. Editors should solicit multiple independent referees and transparently weigh critical reports. Avoid selecting referees or ignoring negative reports to push through a problematic manuscript.
